title: How I developed detective match3 with AI from old PowerPoint
author: General_Correct
selftext:
**After 10+ years as a Google Drive presentation, my game is finally playable.**

Today I finally decided to stop development and release my game. In a post below I have a summary of what was my development and production process for it. Link to the sandbox is in the bottom.  
It’s a mobile-first hybrid of a visual novel and Match-3, inspired by 2000s anime, with a detective story, comedy, a bit of fanservice, and multiple endings. Nothing too fancy, a classic dream game of a teenager that watched too much school anime.   
But the interesting part isn’t really the game itself. It’s how it was made.

**This project is more than 10 years old.**  
Originally, it was just a game concept in a PowerPoint presentation stored on Google Drive. I had ideas for the characters, story, gameplay, and visual direction, but no realistic way to turn everything into a finished game.  
Over the years, I tried several approaches to bringing it to life. Myself and with friends: in plain html and in Unity, Renpy and other engines. Different tools, different implementations, different attempts to find a manageable scope. Some got further than others, but none reached the finish line.  
The script went through multiple rewrites, and frankly, it still needs polishing, especially as English is not my native language.  
For a long time, it was one of those projects I kept coming back to, making some progress, and eventually abandoning again. I’ve even managed to start a career in real gamedev, before finishing this pet-protect, lol.  
Then generative AI started getting good enough to make me reconsider what was possible.

**Building a game with AI**  
Instead of trying to use AI to generate an entire game with a single prompt, I approached it more like managing a small development team.  
I used ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, LM Studio and various coding agents to help with architecture, implementation, refactoring, debugging, documentation, and testing.  
My role was a combination of game designer, producer, art director, and QA tester. I defined the requirements, made design decisions, reviewed the results, tested the builds, and repeatedly sent things back for corrections.  
We started with a browser-based version, eventually making it a mobile-friendly PWA.  
Over time, it grew into a complete visual novel campaign with 22 story cases, three endings, and a connected Match-3 campaign.  
And, unsurprisingly, things broke. A lot.

**GitHub, automated tests, and AI agents**  
One of the most important decisions was to treat this as a proper software development project rather than a collection of AI-generated files. I’ve worked in both IT and gamedev as a manager, so I know how important is to keep everything in order.  
Everything went into GitHub.  
Changes were divided into relatively small tasks and pull requests. GitHub Actions handled automated checks, while GitHub Pages provided separate stable and preview builds.  
We introduced hundreds of automated tests covering game logic, story progression, saves, localization, UI behavior, and more.  
Playwright was particularly useful for browser testing, including Chromium and mobile WebKit.  
I even built a workflow that allowed me to iterate from my iPhone: upload a ZIP containing changes to GitHub, let the pipeline validate it and create a PR, test the preview on my phone, and merge it.  
Of course, having hundreds of tests didn’t mean everything worked.  
We had recurring problems with mobile viewport scaling, safe areas, dialogue pagination, character positioning, and Match-3 animations. Some bugs survived several rounds of fixes. Some fixes introduced new bugs.  
At times, I probably spent more effort debugging AI-generated solutions than it would have taken an experienced developer to implement them properly in the first place.  
But the automated pipeline made the process much more manageable.

**Generating game assets with ComfyUI**  
The art pipeline was another huge experiment.  
I used ComfyUI with local image-generation models, including SD,FLUX, QWEN, Pony, Anima,…to make concepts, create characters, expressions, poses, backgrounds, and other assets.  
The biggest challenge wasn’t generating a good-looking picture.  
It was generating **consistent assets that actually worked together inside a game**.  
Characters needed recognizable faces, consistent proportions, matching art styles, different expressions, and poses that wouldn’t suddenly change their head size or body shape.  
I ended up working with custom ComfyUI workflows, reference images, masking, background removal, and repeated visual comparisons.  
Eventually, we standardized character production around fixed image dimensions, consistent virtual camera positioning, and precomposed expression frames.  
It was still far from perfect. There were plenty of rejected generations, strange anatomy, inconsistent characters, and backgrounds that needed to be regenerated.  
AI image generation saved a lot of work, but it definitely didn’t remove the need for art direction and cleanup. Several characters were completely scrapped from game, several existing ones still require several final touches.

**Then we decided to port the whole thing to Godot**  
Originally, the game was built as a web application.  
Later, I decided to port it to Godot and prepare it for distribution through Playgama.(Don’t ask me why, I think it coated me half of the time and budget).  
This turned out to be a very substantial project.  
It wasn’t a simple export or automatic conversion. We had to reproduce the original game’s systems, UI, story presentation, save functionality, Match-3 mechanics, animations, and other details inside Godot.  
We also introduced automated comparisons between the original web version and the Godot implementation to catch differences in behavior and presentation. I think I will also port most if the tools for Visual Novel and Match3, that I vibe-coded to Godot as well.  
For platform integration, we added the official Playgama Bridge for Godot, prepared the HTML5 export, handled platform lifecycle events, and worked on the packaging and optimization needed for Playgama.  
We also prepared optional rewarded-ad mechanics for things like additional Match-3 moves and hints.  
And today, after all those iterations, I finally got the game into the **Playgama Sandbox**.

**So, was AI actually worth it?**  
For me, absolutely.  
Not because AI wrote perfect code, generated perfect art, or magically understood what I wanted.  
It didn’t.  
AI agents frequently misunderstood requirements, introduced regressions, produced inconsistent implementations, and occasionally overcomplicated surprisingly simple problems.  
But they also allowed me to keep making progress on a project that had been stuck for more than a decade.  
The biggest lesson I learned is that **AI-assisted game development still needs real production processes**.  
Clear requirements, source control, automated testing, documentation, small iterations, manual QA, and the willingness to reject bad results are just as important as the models themselves.  
Maybe even more important.  
And the game isn’t perfect. There are still things I want to improve, especially in the screenplay, presentation, and overall polish.  
This is a Sandbox release, not a big commercial launch. But for a project that spent over ten years as a presentation on Google Drive, having an actual playable version feels like a pretty significant milestone.  
I’m also curious how other developers approach projects like this.  
**Have you tried building a complete game with AI agents? What worked for you, and where did AI create more problems than it solved?**  
And if you try the game, I’d genuinely appreciate feedback — especially on the gameplay, story, and everything   
**Playgama Sandbox:** [https://playgama.ai/play/lstgi4udvqu6bk](https://playgama.ai/play/lstgi4udvqu6bk)
